"We are the daughters of Tariq, walking on carpets."

Al-Qushayri said: The majority hold that "al-tariq" and "al-thaqib" are generic nouns intended in their generality [[That is, no specific star is meant, such as the Pleiades or Saturn, as some exegetes said.]], as we mentioned from Mujahid.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 86, verses 5–8:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So let man look [at] what he was created from﴾, i.e., the son of Adam, from what was he created? The connection with what precedes it: it is an exhortation to man to reflect upon the beginning of his affair and his first state, so that he may know that the One who originated him is able to restore him and to requite him. Then he will act for the Day of Restoration and Recompense, and he will not dictate to his recording angel except what will please him in the outcome of his affair.

"Mimma khuliqa?" (from what was he created?) is an interrogative: from what thing was he created? Then He said, "[He was] created" (khuliqa), which is the answer to the question: ﴿from a gushing fluid﴾, i.e., from the semen (al-maniyy).

Al-Daf'q is the pouring of water. One says: "dafaqtu al-ma' adfuquhu dafqan," meaning "I poured the water." So it is "ma' dafiq," i.e., "madfuq" (poured out), just as they say "sirr katim," meaning "maktum" (concealed), because it derives from your saying "duffiqa al-ma'," in the passive form whose subject is not named. It is not said "dafaqa al-ma'" [Bal yuqal dhalika, wa naqalahu sahib al-Lisan 'an al-Layth. Wa unzur-hu aydan fi al-Misbah al-Munir lil-Fayyumi.] [Rather, that is said; the author of al-Lisan transmitted it from al-Layth. See also al-Misbah al-Munir of al-Fayyumi.] And it is said: "dafaqa Allahu ruhahu," meaning when death is invoked against him.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: ﴿gushing fluid﴾ means poured into the womb. Al-Zajjaj said: "from a water possessing ejaculation (indifaq)." It is said: "dari', faris, and nabil," meaning "dhu faras" (possessor of a horse), "dir'" (armour), and "nabl" (arrows). This is the view of Sibawayh. So "al-dafiq" is that which is ejected with intense force.

He intended two waters: the water of the man and the water of the woman, because the human being is created from both of them. But He made them one water because of their mingling. And it is related from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas: "dafiq" means "viscous" (lazij).

(﴿It emerges﴾) i.e., this water emerges ﴿from between the backbone﴾, i.e., the spine (al-zahr). In it there are four dialects: ṣulb and ṣalb (both recited), ṣalab (with the lam vowelled with a fatha), and ṣalib (on the pattern of qalib). From it is the saying of al-'Abbas: [[He is Ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, praising the Prophet ﷺ; the complete verse is:

"When a generation passes, another appears in its place"]]

"[He] is transferred from loin to womb."

(﴿And the ribs﴾): i.e., the chest. Its singular is "tariba," which is the place of the necklace on the chest. He said:

"Slender, fair, not loose-bellied, / whose ribs are polished like a mirror" [[The verse is from the Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays. Al-muhafhafa: one light of flesh, neither flabby nor large-bellied. Al-mufadha: one whose belly is slack. Al-sajanjal: a mirror. It is said: an ingot of silver, or saffron, or the water of gold.]]

The backbone belongs to the man, and the ribs belong to the woman. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-tara'ib: the place of the necklace." And from him: "what lies between her breasts." 'Ikrimah said the same. It is related from him that "the ribs of the woman" means: the two hands, the two legs, and the two eyes. al-Dahhak said likewise. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the neck. Mujahid said: it is what lies between the two shoulders and the chest. And from him: the chest. And from him: the collarbones (al-taraqi). And from Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "the ribs are four ribs from this side." Al-Zajjaj related that the ribs are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest. Ma'mar ibn Abi Habiba al-Madani said: the ribs are the essence of the heart, and from them the child is produced. The well-known usage of the Arabs is that they are the bones of the chest and the sternum [[In some copies of the original: "that they are the bones of the breast and the chest."]]. Durayd ibn al-Simma said:

"If you turn your backs, we will seize you upon your backs; / if you advance, we will seize you upon the ribs."

Another said:

"She appeared as if the ribs of her throat were / embers of ghada-wood glowing in a forearm."

Another said:

"Saffron upon her ribs, / with which the breasts and the throat are saturated." [[The verse is by al-Khabl. "Shariqa al-jasad bi-l-tib" means the body became full with perfume and constricted. Al-labbat (plural of labba): the place of the necklace.]]

From 'Ikrimah: "al-tara'ib: the chest." Then he recited:

"A string of pearls upon her ribs."

"Mimma khuliqa?" (from what was he created?) is an interrogative: from what thing was he created? Then He said, "[He was] created" (khuliqa), which is the answer to the question: ﴿from a gushing fluid﴾, i.e., from the semen (al-maniyy).

Al-Daf'q is the pouring of water. One says: "dafaqtu al-ma' adfuquhu dafqan," meaning "I poured the water." So it is "ma' dafiq," i.e., "madfuq" (poured out), just as they say "sirr katim," meaning "maktum" (concealed), because it derives from your saying "duffiqa al-ma'," in the passive form whose subject is not named. It is not said "dafaqa al-ma'" [Bal yuqal dhalika, wa naqalahu sahib al-Lisan 'an al-Layth. Wa unzur-hu aydan fi al-Misbah al-Munir lil-Fayyumi.] [Rather, that is said; the author of al-Lisan transmitted it from al-Layth. See also al-Misbah al-Munir of al-Fayyumi.] And it is said: "dafaqa Allahu ruhahu," meaning when death is invoked against him.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: ﴿gushing fluid﴾ means poured into the womb. Al-Zajjaj said: "from a water possessing ejaculation (indifaq)." It is said: "dari', faris, and nabil," meaning "dhu faras" (possessor of a horse), "dir'" (armour), and "nabl" (arrows). This is the view of Sibawayh. So "al-dafiq" is that which is ejected with intense force.

He intended two waters: the water of the man and the water of the woman, because the human being is created from both of them. But He made them one water because of their mingling. And it is related from 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas: "dafiq" means "viscous" (lazij).

(﴿It emerges﴾) i.e., this water emerges ﴿from between the backbone﴾, i.e., the spine (al-zahr). In it there are four dialects: ṣulb and ṣalb (both recited), ṣalab (with the lam vowelled with a fatha), and ṣalib (on the pattern of qalib). From it is the saying of al-'Abbas: [[He is Ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, praising the Prophet ﷺ; the complete verse is:

"When a generation passes, another appears in its place"]]

"[He] is transferred from loin to womb."

(﴿And the ribs﴾): i.e., the chest. Its singular is "tariba," which is the place of the necklace on the chest. He said:

"Slender, fair, not loose-bellied, / whose ribs are polished like a mirror" [[The verse is from the Mu'allaqa of Imru' al-Qays. Al-muhafhafa: one light of flesh, neither flabby nor large-bellied. Al-mufadha: one whose belly is slack. Al-sajanjal: a mirror. It is said: an ingot of silver, or saffron, or the water of gold.]]

The backbone belongs to the man, and the ribs belong to the woman. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-tara'ib: the place of the necklace." And from him: "what lies between her breasts." 'Ikrimah said the same. It is related from him that "the ribs of the woman" means: the two hands, the two legs, and the two eyes. al-Dahhak said likewise. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is the neck. Mujahid said: it is what lies between the two shoulders and the chest. And from him: the chest. And from him: the collarbones (al-taraqi). And from Ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "the ribs are four ribs from this side." Al-Zajjaj related that the ribs are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest. Ma'mar ibn Abi Habiba al-Madani said: the ribs are the essence of the heart, and from them the child is produced. The well-known usage of the Arabs is that they are the bones of the chest and the sternum [[In some copies of the original: "that they are the bones of the breast and the chest."]]. Durayd ibn al-Simma said:

"If you turn your backs, we will seize you upon your backs; / if you advance, we will seize you upon the ribs."

Another said:

"She appeared as if the ribs of her throat were / embers of ghada-wood glowing in a forearm."

Another said:

"Saffron upon her ribs, / with which the breasts and the throat are saturated." [[The verse is by al-Khabl. "Shariqa al-jasad bi-l-tib" means the body became full with perfume and constricted. Al-labbat (plural of labba): the place of the necklace.]]

From 'Ikrimah: "al-tara'ib: the chest." Then he recited:

"A string of pearls upon her ribs."

Dhu al-Rumma said:

"They tore the striped garments from the ribs of a free woman, / and from eyes that slew us every way." [[The complete verse is: "and from eyes that slew us every way."]]

That is, they split. It is also narrated as "darahna" with a ḥā', meaning they threw down. In al-Sihah: "al-tarība" is the singular of al-tara'ib, and they are the bones of the chest, what lies between the collarbone and the nipple. The poet said:

"Her two breasts rose above the tarib."

[[The speaker is al-Aghlab al-'Ijli. The second half of the verse is: "they did not exceed the tafalluk upon the nutub." "Tafallaka" of a girl's breast means it became round. "Al-nutub": the breasts, and it means their elevation.]] Al-Mutaqqib al-'Abdi said:

"And of gold that is polished upon a tarib, / like the colour of ivory, free of wrinkles." [[In some copies and al-Tabari: "yusan"; in some: "yusar" with a ra'. In Ruh al-Ma'ani: "yubayyin" (clarifies). In al-Lisan and Shu'ara' al-Nasraniyya: "yulah" (shines). In al-Lisan, under the root (t-r-b): "... laysa lahu ghudun." The verse is from a qasida with a broken rhyme, beginning:

"Fatima, before your separation, prevent me, / and your refusal of what I asked, as if you would make me..."]]

From other than al-Jawhari: "al-thandawa" for a man is like "al-thady" for a woman. Al-Asma'i said: the place where the breast is attached. Ibn al-Sikkit said: it is the flesh around the breast; if you vowel its first letter with a ḍamma, you hamza it, and if you vowel it with a fatḥa, you do not hamza it [[What is between the brackets is omitted in some copies of the original.]].

In the exegesis: from the man's water which comes out of his backbone come the bone and the sinew, and from the woman's water which comes out of her ribs come the flesh and the blood. This is what al-A'mash said. It has already been transmitted as a marfu' hadith at the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran [[See vol. 4, p. 7]]. And praise be to God. In (al-Hujurat): ﴿We created you from a male and a female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and it has already been discussed [[See vol. 16, p. 343]].

It is said that the man's water descends from the brain, then gathers in the two testicles. This does not contradict His words "from between the backbone," because if it descends from the brain, it passes between the backbone and the ribs.

Qatada said: the meaning is "and it emerges from the backbone of the man and the ribs of the woman." Al-Farra' related that such usage comes from the Arabs, and according to it the meaning of "from between the backbone" is "from the backbone." Al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the backbone of the man and the ribs of the man, and from the backbone of the woman and the ribs of the woman. Then we know that the drop comes from all parts of the body, and for this reason a man resembles his parents greatly [[Al-Ustadh al-Imam said in his tafsir of the juz' 'Amma: "He referred to the backbone as the man, and to the ribs as the woman."]]. This is the wisdom behind washing the whole body after the emission of semen. Also, one who engages much in intercourse feels pain in his back and spine, and this is only because his spine is emptied of the water that had been held in it.

Isma'il related from the people of Makkah: "yakhruju min bayni al-ṣulbi" with a ḍamma on the lam. It is also narrated from 'Isa al-Thaqafi. Al-Mahdawi related it and said: whoever makes the semen emerge from between the backbone of the man and his ribs, the pronoun in "yakhruju" refers to the water. Whoever makes it from between the backbone of the man and the ribs of the woman, the pronoun refers to the human being. It was also recited as "al-ṣalab," with a fatḥa on the ṣād and the lam. In it there are four dialects [[See what preceded on p. 5.]]: ṣulb, ṣalb, ṣalab, and ṣalib. Al-'Ajjaj said:

"In a ṣalab like the well-tanned leather strap."

In praise of the Prophet ﷺ:

"He is transferred from ṣālib to rahim."

[[The complete verse: "when a generation passes, another appears in its place." It is from a saying of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib in praise of the Prophet ﷺ.]] The verses are famous and well known.

Indeed He, may His praise be exalted, ﴿upon its return﴾, i.e., upon returning the water into the urethra, ﴿is truly Able﴾. This is what Mujahid and al-Dahhak said. It is also related from both of them that the meaning is: "Indeed He is able to return the water into the spine." 'Ikrimah said likewise. And from al-Dahhak also: the meaning is: "Indeed He is able to return the human being to water as he was." And from him also: the meaning is: "Indeed He is able to return the human being from old age to youth, and from youth to old age." This is also in al-Mahdawi. In al-Mawardi and al-Tha'labi: "to childhood, and from childhood to the drop." Ibn Zayd said: "Indeed He is able to hold that water back so that it does not come out." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan, and 'Ikrimah also said: "Indeed He is able to return the human being after death." This is the choice of al-Tabari. Al-Tha'labi said: this is the strongest, because of His words, ﴿on the Day when the secrets are examined﴾ [al-Tariq: 9]. Al-Mawardi said: it is possible that it means He will return him to this world after resurrecting him in the Hereafter, because the disbelievers ask God in it for a return.

The first issue: the governing element of "yawma" (on the day), according to the one who takes the meaning to be that He is able to restore the human being, is His saying "laqadir" (is able). "Raj'ihi" (His returning him) does not govern it, because that would separate the silah (the relative clause) from the mawsul (the relative element) with the predicate of "inna" (indeed). According to the other opinions concerning "innahu 'ala raj'ihi laqadir," the governing element of "yawma" is a hidden verb, and "laqadir" does not govern it, because what is meant is [the time] in the world. "Tublá" means "tumtahan wa tukhtabar" (is tested and examined). Abu al-Ghul al-Tuhawi said: [[He is an Islamic-era poet, attributed to "Tuhya," with a dammah on the ta', which is the mother of an Arab tribe.]]

"Wa la tubla basaluhum wa in hum / sallu bil-harbi hinan ba'da hin"

It is also transmitted as "tubla basaluhum." Whoever transmits it as "tublá" with a dammah on the ta' takes it from the sense of testing, and in this transmission "basala" means "al-karahah" (aversion), as if he said: no aversion to it is known from them. "Tublá" also means "ta'rif" (recognition). The reciter (al-rajiz) said:

"Qad kunta qabla al-yawmi tazdirini / fa-al-yawma abluka wa tabtalini"

That is: "I used to know you, and you knew me." Whoever transmits it as "tabla" with a fathah on the ta' means: they do not weaken in war, even if hardships recur upon them time after time, because severe matters, when they recur upon a person, break him and weaken him.

It has also been said: "tublá al-sara'ir" means the hidden things are brought out and manifested, which is everything a person has concealed of good or evil, and what he has kept hidden of faith or disbelief, as al-Ahwas said: [[Thus it appears in some copies of the original, and in Khizanat al-Adab, vol. 1, p. 322. In some copies of the original, and in al-Shi'r wa al-Shu'ara', and in Kitab al-Aghani, vol. 4, p. 242 (Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah edition): "sa-tubla lakum..."]]

"Sa-yabqa laha fi mudmar al-qalbi wa al-hasha / sarirat wuddin yawma tubla al-sara'ir"

The second issue: it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah the Exalted entrusted His creation with four things: prayer, fasting, zakat, and ghusl (ritual washing), and these are the hidden matters which Allah the Mighty and Majestic will test on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Mahdawi mentioned it. Ibn 'Umar said: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever preserves three of them is truly a friend of Allah, and whoever betrays them is truly an enemy of Allah: prayer, fasting, and ghusl from janabah (major impurity)." Al-Tha'labi mentioned it.

Al-Mawardi mentioned from Zayd ibn Aslam: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Trust is threefold: prayer, fasting, and janabah. Allah the Mighty and Majestic entrusted the son of Adam with prayer; if he wishes, he says, 'I prayed,' and he did not pray. Allah the Mighty and Majestic entrusted the son of Adam with fasting; if he wishes, he says, 'I fasted,' and he did not fast. Allah the Mighty and Majestic entrusted the son of Adam with janabah; if he wishes, he says, 'I performed ghusl,' and he did not perform ghusl. Recite, if you wish: 'On the day when the hidden things are tested.'" Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from 'Ata'.

Malik said, in the transmission of Ashhab from him, when I asked him about the words of the Exalted: "On the day when the hidden things are tested": "Has it reached you that wudu' (ablution) is among the hidden things?" He said: "That has reached me in what people say. As for a hadith I narrate, no." Prayer is among the hidden things, and fasting is among the hidden things; if he wishes, he says, "I prayed," and he did not pray. And among the hidden things is what is in the hearts, for which Allah will recompense His servants.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: Ibn Mas'ud said: "The martyr is forgiven for everything except trust (amanah). Wudu' is of trust, prayer and zakat are of trust, and the deposit (wadi'ah) is of trust, and the gravest of these is the deposit. It will be represented to him in the form it had on the day he took it, and he will be thrown with it into the bottom of Hell. It will be said to him, 'Bring it out,' and he will follow it, and place it on his neck. When he hopes to come out with it, it slips from him, and he follows it again; he remains so for the age of ages."

Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: "Among trust is that a woman is entrusted with her private part." Ashhab said: Sufyan said to me: concerning menstruation and pregnancy, if she says, "I did not menstruate, and I am pregnant," she is believed, so long as she does not produce something that shows she is lying.

And in the hadith: "Janabah ghusl is of trust."

Ibn 'Umar said: On the Day of Resurrection Allah will reveal every hidden secret, so it will be an adornment on some faces and a disgrace on other faces. Allah knows everything, but He will manifest the signs of the angels and the believers.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then he will have no power﴾, meaning the human being will have no strength, that is, no defense that protects him, ﴿nor any helper﴾ to help him against what has befallen him.

It is related from Ikrimah regarding ﴿Then he will have no power nor any helper﴾ that he said: "These kings, on the Day of Resurrection, will have no power nor any helper."

Sufyan said: "The power (quwwah) is the clan (ʿashirah), and the helper (nasir) is the ally (halif)."

It was also said: "﴿Then he will have no power﴾ in his own body, and ﴿nor any helper﴾ from others by whom he may defend himself against Allah." This is the meaning given by Qatadah.

(ﷺ) Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 86, verses 11–16:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By the sky which returns﴾, meaning the sky that has rain. It returns every year with rain after rain. This is what the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun, scholars of tafsir) have said. The lexicographers (ahl al-lugha) said: al-raj' means rain. They cited, as evidence, al-Mutanakhkhil describing a sword, which he likened to water:

A white one like rain, deep-sinking when it plunges into a ... which cuts through the flesh.

Its foot sank into the mud: tha'at, yathuthu and yathiku mean it went in and was submerged in it. This is what al-Jawhari said. [[What is between the brackets is noted in the margin of some copies of the original. Al-muhtafal: the largest part of the body. Yakhtali: cuts.]] Al-Khalil said: al-raj' is the rain itself, and al-raj' is also the spring vegetation. It was said: ﴿which returns﴾ means ﴿which benefits﴾. Rain may also be called awb, just as it is called raj', as one poet said:

A lofty, towering height, to whose summit none ascends except the clouds and the awb and the sabl.

[[The line is by al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhali. Al-Sukkari said in his commentary on this line: "Raba' — one climbs up to it. He says: none draws near to its summit, i.e., its top. That is, none rises to this hill because of its height except the clouds and the awb. Al-awb: the return of the bees. Al-sabl: the rain when it pours down."]]

(Margin) Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the sun, the moon and the stars return in the sky; they rise from one direction and set in another. It was also said: ﴿which returns﴾ refers to the angels, because they return to it with the deeds of the servants. This is an oath.

(And by the earth which splits open) is another oath, meaning that it splits open for the plants, the trees, the fruits and the rivers. Its parallel is: ﴿Then We split the earth, splitting [it]﴾ [Abasa: 26], and so on. Al-sad' means al-shaqq (splitting), because it splits the earth and the earth splits by it. It is as if He said: ﴿by the earth which has plants﴾, because the plant splits the earth. Mujahid said: ﴿by the earth which has the paths that walkers split﴾. It was also said: ﴿which has tilling﴾, because it splits it. It was also said: ﴿which has the dead﴾, because they split open from it for the resurrection.

(Indeed, it is a decisive word) The oath is sworn on this: that the Qur'an distinguishes between truth and falsehood. In the introduction of this book [[See vol. 1, p. 5, second or third printing.]] has already been mentioned what al-Harith narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "It is a Book containing the news of what came before you and the judgment of what comes after you. It is the decisive word, not a jest. Whoever abandons it out of arrogance, Allah will break him, and whoever seeks guidance in other than it, Allah will lead him astray." It was also said: the meaning of ﴿decisive word﴾ is the threat mentioned earlier in this surah, in His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾, ﴿the Day when secrets are examined﴾.

(And it is not a jest) meaning the Qur'an is not falsehood and play. Al-hazl is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness), and hazala, yahzilu [means to jest]. Al-Kumayt said:

He makes us strive every day and we jest. [[The first half of the line: "We see ourselves, in love of life and its length..."]]

﴿Indeed, they plot a plot﴾, meaning the enemies of Allah plot a plot, that is, they scheme against Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions with a scheme.

(And I plot a plot) meaning I will repay them the recompense of their plotting. It was also said: it is what Allah inflicted upon them on the day of Badr of killing and capture. It was also said: the plotting of Allah is leading them gradually, from where they do not know. This meaning has already been discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, at His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 15], and has been fully treated there. [[See vol. 1, p. 208, second or third printing.]]

**God Almighty's words: ﴿So leave the disbelievers alone﴾**, meaning: delay them, and do not ask God to hasten their destruction. **﴿And be patient with what He arranges﴾** concerning their affairs. (In some copies: "what He wills.") Then it was **abrogated (naskh)** by the verse of the sword: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (At-Tawbah: 5). **Amhilhum** (﴿leave them﴾) is an emphatic form. *Mahhala* and *amhala* have the same meaning, like *nazzala* and *anzala*. *Amhilhu* means "give him respite," and *mahhilhu tamhilan* is the verbal noun, and the noun is *al-muhlah* (respite). *Al-istimhal* means seeking respite. *Tamahhala fi amrihi* means he took his time in his affair. *Itmahalla, itmihlalan* means he straightened up and stood erect. *Al-itmihlal* also means calm and slackening. It is said: *mahlan ya fulan*, meaning "gently and calmly." **Ruwaydan** means "a little," according to Ibn 'Abbas. Qatadah said: "slowly." The implied meaning is: delay them a slight delay. In the speech of the Arabs, *ruwayd* is the diminutive of *rawd*, and Abu 'Ubayd said the same. He recited:

*Ka'annaha thamilun yamshi 'ala rud*
*(As if she were a drunkard walking slowly)*

This is the second half of a line by al-Jumuh al-Zafari, whose first half is:

*Takadu la tathlimu al-batha'a wati'ha*
*(She almost does not dent the valley floor with her tread)*

That is, *'ala mahal*, meaning "at a leisurely pace." The explanation of *ruwaydan* is *mahlan* ("slowly"). The explanation of *ruwaydaka* is *amhil* ("give respite"), because the *kaf* is only attached when it has the sense of an imperative (*af'il*) and not otherwise. The letter *dal* was vowelled because two unvowelled letters came together, so it was put in the accusative like verbal nouns. It is a diminutive used as a command, because it is the diminutive of the abbreviated form of *irwad*, which is the verbal noun of *arwada yurwidu*.

It has four uses: as a verb-like noun (*ism li-l-fi'l*), as an adjective (*sifah*), as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and as a verbal noun (*masdar*). As a verb-like noun, as in your saying: *ruwayda 'Amran*, meaning *arwid 'Amran*, that is, "give 'Amr respite." As an adjective, as in your saying: *saru sayran ruwayadan* ("they travelled a gentle journey"). As a circumstantial accusative, as in your saying: *sara al-qawmu ruwayadan* ("the people travelled slowly"); when it is attached to a definite noun, it becomes a circumstantial accusative for it. As a verbal noun, as in your saying: *ruwayda 'Amrin* with the genitive by annexation, like His words: ﴿so strike the necks﴾ (Muhammad: 4). Al-Jawhari said all of this.

In the verse, of these uses, the most fitting is that it be an adjective of the verbal noun, meaning: "a gentle respite." It may also be a circumstantial accusative, meaning: "give them respite without hastening their punishment for them."

**The surah ends.**
